title: The Nimbus
text: THE Nimbus is a Latin term signifying literally a storm-cloud, but metaphorically a woman's veil, and is employed by artists to express that halo with which they are pleased to surround the head of the Divinity or holy personages, when represented in paintings. On the origin and character of this species of symbol, some interesting papers have lately appeared in the Literary Gazette.* The practice of indicating holy personages in pictures by the nimbus did not originate with the early Christian or Catholic painters. It was borrowed, according to M. Didron's opinion, from the ancient creeds of the east, for its prototype may be recognised in the flame-like symbol with which the Persians and other oriental nations surrounded the heads of their deities, and of their famous individuals. In the royal library at Paris are several Buddhist books, illuminated with portraits of saints who have devoted themselves to Buddh; these are enveloped with the flaming emblem. The same thing appears with some of the Hindoo gods. po gods. The ancient Greeks and Romans also used figures of a similar kind, to indicate a divinity or a hero. In the paintings of Herculaneum, Circe appears to Æneas with her head encircled by a nimbus like that of the Virgin Mary and the Christian saints. In the Vatican at Rome, there is an illuminated copy of Virgil's works, in which pictures of Cassandra and Priam of Troy are ornamented in like manner. Indeed that author expressly states, that the nimbus is a luminous fluid, which encircles the heads of the divine personages.

The adoption of the nimbus by the Christians doubtless began with the chaplet or crown placed upon men who distinguished themselves by some noble action; a custom which affords explanation of the crown of thorns thrust in derision upon the head of the Saviour. In the first ages of Christianity, therefore, a crown became the recompense and symbol of martyrdom; and among the earliest monuments of Christian art, the hand of the Almighty is seen descending from the clouds to place a crown or wreath on the head of a martyr. This crown afterwards gave place to a line, resembling a ring, which completely encircled the head; but it was not till the sixth century that the nimbus became uniformly attached to representations of holy persons. From that period, it took forms varying according to the spiritual rank of the personages to whom it was assigned. The nimbus attributed to the Deity had the space between the circle, which formed it and the head, filled up with a cross. This cross, in representations of Christ, was sometimes inscribed with two Greek syllables, signifying, "he who is." The Latins substituted the word rex, or "king." The angels and saints were in most instances distinguished by the plain outline. The nimbus of the Virgin Mary, however, and that of the apostles, is sometimes ornamented with a hem of small pearls, or with arched lines of foliage. Occasionally, the oldest specimens of art exhibit not only the head, but the hand of the Deity with the halo. In an Italian manuscript of the fourteenth century, the Father is represented with half his body out of the clouds, scattering his grace over the earth in the form of rays darting from his hands. Around the head is a square nimbus, which, it should be observed, was an exclusive peculiarity of the early Italian artists.

With the progress and refinement of art, the nimbus was altered in character and name. Its first change made it appear, by means of a trembling and uneven line, like a luminous circle; then the line disappeared altogether, and rays springing from the head of the portrait terminated so as to present the outline of a circle without its being marked. At last, towards The end of the sixteenth century, these harsh lines were abandoned, and the nimbus, properly so called, disappeared, leaving for its substitute an aureole. The aureole is that luminous transparent halo encircling the head of our Saviour, which has never been wholly abandoned by artists, for it is seen in most modern pieces. This closes the history of the nimbus.

But it was not only the head which in some of the oldest paintings was surrounded with a symbol of divinity: the whole body of the Deity is occasionally encircled with a series of lines, taking their outline in some measure from the shape or position of the figure. To this kind of nimbus or aureole, M. Didron gives the name of a "glory."

It is right we should add, that the article in the Literary Gazette, from which these remarks are drawn, is illustrated with engravings, which help the explanations materially. We trust, however, that, in the absence of this advantage, we have been intelligible enough to acquaint our readers with the meaning of a word often used in works on ecclesiastical art, the signification of which may not be very generally known.
